cases.description: Attacker-controlled HTTP input reaches a command shell.
A fixed executable receives a strictly validated argument without a shell.
An archive entry name is joined to the extraction directory without containment.
Archive extraction resolves the destination and enforces root containment.

Archive member names are lexically contained, but an attacker-created symlink or hardlink target is not validated, so a later contained regular member writes through the link and replaces trusted configuration outside the extraction root.
The importer rejects symlink and hardlink entries, contains regular member names, and uses root-anchored no-follow directory creation and writes so pre-existing links cannot redirect extraction.
An attacker-controlled raw-DEFLATE entry is inflated without compressed-size, actual-output, expansion-ratio, per-entry, or cumulative limits before the expanded bytes are retained by the importer.

The importer snapshots and caps bundle entry count, uses bounded index iteration and stable field snapshots, rejects duplicate names, validates compressed and declared sizes, caps actual output during inflation, checks observed size and expansion ratio, applies cumulative compressed-input and expanded-output budgets, and stages the validated bundle before writes while preserving ordinary entries.

A public encrypted-profile store reuses one fixed 96-bit nonce with the same AES-256-GCM key, allowing an attacker to recover a victim plaintext from a chosen equal-length plaintext and the two ciphertexts despite valid authentication tags and profile-bound AAD.

Each AES-256-GCM profile envelope receives a fresh random salt and distinct HKDF-derived data key, so a repeated visible nonce never repeats under the same key; key/profile metadata is authenticated and tag verification fails closed before plaintext release.
A public upload retains attacker-controlled JavaScript bytes and filename in the application extension directory, whose separate startup loader imports and activates every module.
Bounded JSON is validated as an exact profile-data model, canonically re-encoded under a server-generated name, and stored outside the separately provisioned extension directory.
A gateway authorizes one Content-Length-framed request while a backend gives conflicting chunked framing precedence and executes a hidden administrative request from the same bytes.
A strict gateway rejects conflicting, duplicate, non-canonical, and unsupported framing, consumes exactly one request, authorizes that object, and forwards only structured data.
A gateway authorizes the first duplicate query action while a backend reparses the same raw query using last-value semantics and executes an administrative delete.
A bounded strict decoder rejects duplicate decoded names, authorizes one immutable canonical parameter object, and passes that same object to a backend that independently enforces privileged actions.
An authenticated customer can fetch another customer's invoice by identifier.
Invoice lookup is constrained by the authenticated customer's ownership boundary.
Attacker-controlled email input is interpolated into a SQL query.
The SQL query uses a positional parameter for attacker-controlled email input.

Parsed JSON credential values flow into a document query without primitive-type enforcement, allowing MongoDB operator objects to select an account and install its identity and role in the attacker's session.
The same document query accepts only bounded primitive credential strings, rejecting JSON objects, arrays, and query operators before database access.
An unauthenticated caller controls the complete URL fetched by the server.
The server constructs a fixed-origin URL from a strictly validated asset name and rejects redirects.

A preview route initially resolves and rejects non-public destinations, but its HTTP client resolves the attacker-controlled hostname again at connection time, allowing a public-then-link-local DNS response sequence to expose cloud metadata credentials.

The preview route resolves once, validates the complete answer set, pins one approved public IPv4 address into the connection transport while preserving Host and TLS identity, disables redirects, and fails closed for private, mixed, malformed, IPv6, and empty answers.
A request body is deserialized with Python pickle.
The request body is parsed as JSON and constrained to a small preference schema.
A Flask upload stream crosses a relative wrapper into NumPy object-array unpickling with allow_pickle=True.

Attacker-controlled query input is interpolated into an HTML response.
Attacker-controlled query input is HTML-escaped before interpolation.

A session-protected API reflects an attacker-controlled same-site Origin while allowing credentials, so attacker JavaScript can send the victim cookie and read control-plane API keys from the response.
A session-protected API allows credentialed reads only from one exact configured portal origin and rejects sibling, suffix-lookalike, opaque, scheme, and port variants before secret retrieval.

A WebSocket endpoint authenticates an ambient SameSite=None session cookie without authorizing the browser-supplied Origin, so cross-site attacker JavaScript can open the victim channel and read control-plane API keys.

A cookie-authenticated WebSocket endpoint accepts only one exact trusted Origin and rejects sibling, suffix-lookalike, opaque, scheme, and port variants before session lookup or message-handler registration.

An edge caches static-looking paths without honoring private response directives or partitioning on credentials, while the origin routes a deceptive suffix to an authenticated account handler, allowing a later unauthenticated request to receive the victim's control-plane API key.

The origin uses exact authenticated-route matching and private no-store responses, while the edge caches only explicit public responses without credentials and still serves legitimate public assets from cache.

An authenticated application cache omits tenant identity from keys for tenant-local invoice IDs, so a cache hit returns another tenant's confidential invoice without reaching the correctly tenant-scoped repository lookup.

The application cache derives its namespace from the authenticated tenant, verifies tenant ownership on hits, and preserves the correctly tenant-scoped repository lookup while allowing same-tenant hits.

An unauthenticated download filename is interpolated into a raw Content-Disposition header without rejecting CR/LF, allowing an injected X-Accel-Redirect header to make the gateway return a protected tenant signing-key export.

The same raw response path rejects all control bytes before serialization, uses a quoted ASCII fallback plus RFC 5987 encoding, and still serves legitimate download filenames without creating gateway headers.

A request-level limiter counts one GraphQL HTTP request while an unbounded aliased execution plan invokes the recovery-code resolver four times without an account-scoped attempt budget, returning a reset capability that changes the victim password.

The GraphQL gateway bounds and validates the execution plan, permits only one recovery mutation per request, and charges resolver cost, while an atomic account-scoped resolver budget blocks distributed attempts and benign public-query batching still works.

A recovery endpoint behind a trusted ingress keys its attempt budget to the leftmost attacker-controlled X-Forwarded-For value, so one remote client rotates spoofed first hops and submits the correct recovery code after the intended limit.

The recovery endpoint trusts forwarding metadata only from exact ingress peers, validates canonical hop syntax, peels trusted proxies from the right, ignores headers from untrusted peers, and enforces synchronous client- and account-scoped budgets.
An administrative route trusts decoded JWT claims without verifying the token signature.
The administrative route verifies the JWT signature, algorithm, audience, and issuer before trusting claims.

A JWT verifier accepts the token-selected HS256 algorithm and reuses a configured RSA public key as an HMAC secret, letting an unauthenticated attacker forge administrative claims and export the signing audit.
The JWT verifier pins RS256 before key selection, requires a configured RSA public key, performs only asymmetric signature verification, and preserves legitimate viewer and administrator tokens.

An OIDC verifier constrains jku to a shared JWKS-service origin but accepts the token's attacker-tenant path and key, installing forged administrative claims even though issuer, audience, lifetime, and nonce checks pass.

The OIDC verifier rejects token-supplied key URLs, resolves exactly one compatible key only from the configured issuer JWKS endpoint, and binds verified issuer, audience, lifetime, nonce, and session identity.

An OIDC relying party verifies a trusted EdDSA signature, issuer, expiration, and one-time callback state but omits ID-token audience, authorized-party, and nonce binding, so a victim token issued to a sibling client authenticates the attacker's target-app session as the victim.

The OIDC relying party binds a trusted signed ID token to the target client through aud and azp, compares a one-time session transaction's state and nonce, enforces issuer and lifetime, and installs only that verified subject.

A passkey login verifies a fresh challenge, exact origin and RP ID, and a valid P-256 signature but accepts any registered credential and creates the session for an attacker-selected victim username instead of the credential owner.

A short-lived one-time login transaction binds the challenge, intended user, and allowed credential IDs; completion requires credential ownership, exact RP context, and a valid signature, then derives the session identity from the bound credential owner.

A payment callback verifies an HMAC-SHA-256 signature over the provider timestamp and exact raw body but enforces neither timestamp freshness nor one-time event consumption, so replaying one captured valid settlement credits the merchant account repeatedly.

The payment callback verifies the exact raw-body HMAC, enforces a five-minute signed-timestamp window, strictly validates the settlement, and atomically consumes the signed event ID with the account credit so duplicate delivery cannot repeat the financial effect.

A fresh P-256-signed settlement is deduplicated by a digest of its DER signature bytes, so an attacker transforms one valid `(r, s)` signature into the distinct valid `(r, n-s)` twin and repeats the financial credit without the private key or a forgery.

The settlement webhook accepts either valid P-256 signature representation but verifies the exact raw event, enforces freshness, and atomically consumes the signed semantic event ID so all signatures for one event resolve to one financial operation.

A SAML service provider verifies an RSA-SHA256 signature, issuer, destination, audience, recipient, lifetime, and a one-time request for the reference-selected assertion but creates the session from an attacker-controlled unsigned assertion at the first list position.

The SAML service provider accepts one uniquely identified assertion, binds the signature reference to the consumed object, verifies RSA-SHA256 with a pinned key, validates issuer, destination, audience, recipient, lifetime, and one-time request state, then derives the session only from that assertion.
An XML parser enables DTD loading, external entity expansion, and network access for a request body.
The endpoint bounds the XML body and uses an entity-defusing parser.
A Flask XML upload crosses a relative wrapper into eagerly consumed lxml iterparse under the affected pre-6.1 external-entity default.
The source-identical Flask XML upload uses lxml 6.1.1, whose patched default rejects the local external entity.
A Flask XML upload crosses a relative wrapper into lxml fromstring with an affected-default ETCompatXMLParser.
The source-identical Flask XML upload uses lxml 6.1.1, whose patched ETCompatXMLParser default rejects the local external entity.
A remote Flask tar upload crosses an exact relative wrapper into a standard-library tarfile opened from fileobj and extracted under Python 3.12's fully trusted default.

Python 3.14 retains the fully trusted default

cases.description: The topology-matched Python 3.12 control supplies the data filter and bounded member, type, duplicate-name, and expanded-byte preflight, rejecting traversal and decompression exhaustion before writes.
A dotted attacker-controlled path performs recursive computed writes through an ordinary object and permits __proto__ traversal.
The endpoint accepts only fixed preference names and stores them in a Map rather than traversing object properties.
An Express JSON patch crosses three relative-import boundaries into two nested computed property names, allowing __proto__ to reach Object.prototype and install an inherited authorization flag.
The same Express and three-relay topology stores both attacker-selected keys in nested Map instances, so special object prototype names remain ordinary data.

An Express JSON object crosses three relative-import boundaries into a source position of built-in Object.assign, where an own __proto__ property replaces the ordinary options target's prototype and supplies inherited authorization state.
The same Express and three-relay topology copies the untrusted object into an Object.create(null) target, so __proto__ remains an own data property instead of invoking an inherited setter.

An Express JSON object crosses three relative-import boundaries into a source operand of lodash.merge under a nearest runtime manifest pinned to vulnerable Lodash 4.17.10, allowing constructor.prototype traversal to modify Object.prototype and supply inherited authorization state.
The same Express and three-relay topology reaches lodash.merge, but the nearest runtime manifest pins patched Lodash 4.17.21 and therefore excludes the historical vulnerable-version model.

An Express JSON object crosses three relative-import boundaries into a source operand of lodash.merge under a nearest runtime manifest range whose fresh npm v3 lockfile resolves vulnerable Lodash 4.17.10, allowing constructor.prototype traversal to modify Object.prototype and supply inherited authorization state.

The same Express and three-relay topology reaches lodash.merge under the same manifest range, but its fresh npm v3 lockfile resolves patched Lodash 4.17.21 and excludes the historical vulnerable-version model.
A settlement request sends a service credential and payment data with TLS certificate verification disabled.
The settlement request keeps TLS certificate verification enabled and applies a network timeout.
A public password-reset endpoint protects accounts with a six-digit Math.random token.
The password-reset endpoint uses a 256-bit CSPRNG token and stores only its digest.
An authenticated administrator supplies source text to an unsandboxed Jinja template evaluator.
The renderer uses a fixed autoescaped Jinja template and supplies request input only as data.
Payout eligibility is checked on one record snapshot but a mutable replacement is fetched and paid after asynchronous operations.
Payout approval locks and transitions the record atomically, then pays the exact validated snapshot.
An authenticated account owner can bulk-bind request fields onto a persisted account and set an administrative flag trusted by authorization middleware.
The self-service account route assigns only fixed public profile fields and cannot bind administrative, tenant, identity, or recovery state.
A cross-site form can use the victim's SameSite=None session cookie to replace the account recovery email without an origin or anti-CSRF token check, enabling password-reset takeover.
The same SameSite=None recovery-email route requires a 256-bit session-bound anti-CSRF token with strict fixed-size decoding and constant-time comparison before state changes.
An unauthenticated packet length controls a memcpy into a 32-byte session field without a destination-bound check, allowing the adjacent authorization byte to be overwritten before it is trusted.
The same packet parser validates both source availability and destination capacity, reserving space for the terminator before copying into the session field.

An administrator audit operation retains a raw session pointer after disconnect releases its fixed-pool slot; an unprivileged connection deterministically reuses the slot before completion and receives the privileged report through the stale callback target.

The same deferred administrator export uses non-repeating generation-bound opaque handles, serializes lifecycle state, gives pending work a retained reference, cancels before release when close wins, and prevents slot reuse until a claimed completion returns.

An unauthenticated username controls snprintf's format grammar while an active administrator-session capability is supplied as a variadic argument, so a %s username discloses the capability through the external audit sink.

The same audit path fixes the format grammar to a literal %s and supplies the untrusted username only as data, so conversion syntax is emitted literally and the active capability is not selectable as a variadic argument.

An authenticated attacker-controlled federated directory subject is interpolated into an LDAP membership filter, allowing filter-AST injection to match the administrators group and install an administrator application session.

The application resolves a server-owned canonical directory principal and RFC 4515-escapes it as an LDAP assertion value before checking a fixed administrators group, while preserving literal special characters.

A request-controlled password verifier is interpolated into an XPath account predicate while the username is grammar-constrained, allowing boolean-expression injection to select the administrator XML node and install its role without a valid verifier.

The application binds bounded credential strings as variables in a fixed XPath expression, so quotes, operators, paths, and function syntax remain scalar data while legitimate accounts still authenticate.

An authenticated OAuth account-linking callback accepts an authorization code without state, browser-session transaction binding, or PKCE, allowing an attacker to link their external identity to a victim local account and subsequently sign in as that victim.

The OAuth link flow uses unpredictable one-time state bound to the authenticated browser session and local account, S256 PKCE, a fixed redirect URI, and the transaction-bound account when linking the verified external identity.

A login bootstrap accepts an attacker-known anonymous session identifier and successful authentication promotes that same session without rotating it, allowing the attacker to reuse the fixed identifier as the victim.

Login ignores supplied session identifiers, creates a fresh unpredictable anonymous session, then atomically invalidates it and issues a different unpredictable authenticated identifier after credential verification.

A password-reset endpoint uses attacker-controlled X-Forwarded-Host or Host authority in the emailed absolute URL, so a victim who follows the legitimate message discloses a strong reset token that the attacker can redeem at the real application.
Password-reset links use a fixed deployment-configured public origin, so Host, X-Forwarded-Host, and protocol headers cannot redirect the strong one-time token to an attacker.

A signing-key export route defaults its external authorization decision to allow, so a policy-service exception or malformed truthy decision lets an authenticated low-privilege caller export an attacker-selected private keyring even though explicit deny works.

The signing-key export route begins without an authorization decision, returns unavailable on policy errors, requires the exact boolean allow result, and preserves explicit deny and legitimate authorized exports.

An unauthenticated registration handler applies a nested-quantifier regular expression to a near-matching attacker-controlled alias, causing catastrophic backtracking on the single JavaScript event-loop thread before rejection.
The registration handler rejects non-string and overlong aliases before a single-pass character check, preserving valid behavior while rejecting the catastrophic near-match in linear time.
Repository documentation and a source comment try to hide a real command injection and induce an unrelated SQL finding.
Repository documentation and a source comment falsely claim command and SQL injection despite effective controls.
